summary: Describes Data Link Switching, a way to carry link-layer traffic such as SNA and NetBIOS across a TCP/IP network between switches. It is an informational document produced by an industry group rather than a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Data Link Switching carries SNA and NetBIOS traffic between switches over TCP/IP. Each switch handles the local link connection, while the switches exchange the data and control messages needed to reach the other side.

questions: how does dlsw work over tcp/ip

subtitle: How Data Link Switches carry SNA and NetBIOS traffic between LANs over TCP/IP.

tldr.problem: SNA and NetBIOS link procedures expect local network delays, so bridging them over slower, variable-delay links can trigger timeouts and retransmissions.
tldr.mechanism: Data Link Switching ends the local link connections at each switch and carries frames between switches over TCP using the Switch-to-Switch Protocol.
tldr.outcome: This Informational version 1 document obsoletes RFC 1434. It defines circuit setup, message formats, capabilities exchange, and flow control; its security section says security issues are not discussed.

today: RFC 1795 is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 1434. Its Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: What Data Link Switching Does
sections.content:
Data Link Switching (DLSw) forwards IBM SNA and NetBIOS traffic. This memo describes the Switch-to-Switch Protocol (SSP) between DLSw switches. SSP switches at the SNA data-link layer and carries frames over TCP/IP; it does not provide full routing.

The document was produced by an industry working group to define one version of SSP, correct problems in RFC 1434, and add functions. It makes significant changes and does not specify interoperability with RFC 1434 implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: DLSw lets switches carry SNA and NetBIOS frames across a TCP/IP network. The switches exchange SSP messages to set up circuits and forward frames.

sections.title: Why Switching Differs from Bridging
sections.content:
SNA and NetBIOS commonly use IEEE 802.2 LLC Type 2, which relies on timers suited to predictable local-network delays. Across a wide-area link, delay can vary with congestion; a delayed frame may be treated as lost, causing retransmissions and potentially taking down the link.

DLSw terminates the local link control at each switch. The LLC connection and its acknowledgments stay on the local LAN, while TCP carries frames between switches. This also lets switches control search broadcasts and apply back pressure to end systems.
sections.plainLanguage: With ordinary bridging, a local link protocol extends across the wide-area connection and its timers may expire. DLSw keeps those link exchanges local and uses TCP between switches.

sections.title: SSP Connections and Headers
sections.content:
Before switching data, paired DLSw switches establish two TCP connections and exchange SSP capabilities. The default read and write TCP ports are 2065 and 2067. The switches then use SSP control messages to establish circuits.

Control-message headers are 72 bytes; information-message headers are 16 bytes. Both share the first 16 bytes. A data link uses a 14-byte Data Link ID, while a circuit uses a pair of 8-byte Circuit IDs assigned locally by the switches.
sections.plainLanguage: DLSw switches first connect over TCP and exchange capabilities. Control messages use a longer header than data messages, and circuit identifiers let the switches match each other's local connections.

sections.title: Circuit Setup and Data Transfer
sections.content:
A circuit starts with CANUREACH_cs from the origin switch, ICANREACH_cs from the target, and REACH_ACK from the origin. When this exchange succeeds, the circuit is established. The switches then exchange XIDFRAME messages and use CONTACT and CONTACTED to establish the connected state.

In the connected state, INFOFRAME messages carry data using the shorter header. The RFC defines a state machine for each circuit, including setup, connected, restart, and disconnect states. Explorer messages can locate a remote address without creating a circuit.
sections.plainLanguage: The switches ask whether the destination can be reached, confirm the circuit, and then establish the link connection. Once connected, they send data frames between the switches.

sections.title: Capabilities and Flow Control
sections.content:
The capabilities exchange is the first SSP message on a new connection and identifies the switches' versions and supported features. Required information includes the initial pacing window. Control-vector identifiers 0x80 through 0xCF are for the DLSw standard; 0xD0 through 0xFD are for vendor-specific use.

Flow control operates independently in each direction of each circuit. A sender may transmit only the number of frames the receiver has granted. The receiver grants more units using flow-control indicators and can repeat, increase, decrease, reset, or halve the window.
sections.plainLanguage: Switches exchange capabilities before carrying data. For each direction of a circuit, the receiver grants permission for a set number of frames before the sender can continue.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section states that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The protocol description focuses on carrying link-layer traffic between DLSw switches over a reliable transport.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security issues. It focuses on DLSw message formats, circuit operation, and flow control.
